opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something to the charge, but I don't think it's quite right, and the reason is interesting.

It's true that historically we've kept moving the goalposts. People said a machine that could beat the world chess champion would be intelligent; then it happened and we said, "well, that's just search." The same happened with Go, with passing something like a Turing test in casual conversation, and now with mathematics. So I'm sympathetic to the worry that every time AI clears a bar, we quietly raise it.

But I think there's a different reading of what's going on. Proving a novel mathematical result at an expert level is extraordinarily impressive, and in some ways it's harder than running a cafe; very few humans can do it. But it's a particular kind of task: well-specified, verifiable, done over a bounded period, in a domain where the system gets clear feedback. Running a cafe is "easy" for humans in a very different sense. It requires sustained agency over weeks and months, dealing with suppliers who don't reply, a fridge that breaks, a staff member who calls in sick, a customer who's upset, a council regulation you didn't know about. It's open-ended, messy, and long-horizon, and the errors compound if you aren't tracking them.

What we're discovering is that intelligence isn't a single dial. Systems can be superhuman on the peaks and still surprisingly weak in the valleys. The word "general" in artificial general intelligence was always meant to capture breadth: the ability to handle the whole range of things a competent adult can handle, not just the hardest-seeming intellectual feats. So asking whether it can run a cafe isn't so much raising the bar as testing a dimension the maths benchmark never measured.

And that matters for thinking about risk and transformative impact. Much of what would make AI truly world-changing, for better or worse, depends on that kind of reliable, autonomous, long-horizon competence in the real world, rather than brilliance on a self-contained problem. So I'd say the cafe test isn't moving the goalposts; it's pointing out that there were always several sets of goalposts, and we'd only been watching one of them.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts expert-level mathematical proofs with running a café, but does not state that people expected AI to be able to run a café by the time it could prove novel mathematical results.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a fair challenge, and I want to take it seriously rather than just wave it away. If you'd told someone in 2015 that a system would be proving novel results at the level of a strong mathematician, they'd have said, obviously that's AGI, we're done. So there is something uncomfortable about then saying, well, but can it run a cafe? It does look like the goalposts are moving.

But I think what's actually happened is that we've learned something about which capabilities were really the hard ones, and that's a legitimate kind of update. Our intuitions about difficulty were calibrated on humans. For humans, proving research-level theorems is extremely rare and running a cafe is something millions of people manage, so we assumed the theorem was the summit and the cafe was the foothills. It turns out that's just a fact about the human profile of abilities, not a fact about the tasks themselves. Mathematics has a very clean structure: well-specified goals, short feedback loops, you can verify a proof, you can generate huge amounts of training signal. Running a cafe involves long time horizons, messy physical and social environments, dealing with the supplier who hasn't shown up, the staff member who's quit, remembering what happened three weeks ago and why it matters now. Those are exactly the things current systems are weakest at.

So I'd distinguish two things. One is the question of whether a system is impressive, or superhuman in some domain, and I'd say yes, clearly, and we shouldn't minimise it. The other is whether it's general in the sense the term was originally meant to capture, which was really something like: can it do the broad range of economically relevant tasks that a competent person can do? And on that reading, the cafe example isn't a new demand; it's closer to the original meaning than the maths benchmark was. The maths benchmark was always a proxy, and it's turned out to be a worse proxy than we thought.

Where I'd concede ground is that people shouldn't be allowed to do this indefinitely. If every time a milestone is reached we invent a new one, the concept becomes unfalsifiable and useless, and critics are right to be suspicious. So I think the honest thing to say is: this is a genuine case where our definition was underspecified, we should now state fairly concretely what we mean, something like reliably performing long-horizon tasks across most jobs with the autonomy of a human employee, and then hold ourselves to it. And it's worth noticing that on the timelines question, this cuts both ways. The fact that the hard-looking things fell first doesn't mean the easy-looking things are far off. It might just mean our map of what's hard was wrong, and the cafe could fall sooner than its difficulty for current systems suggests.

r001.rationale: The response says people treated research-level theorem proving as the summit and running a café as the foothills, implying they expected café-running to be within reach by the time AI proved expert-level novel results.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between moving the goalposts and pointing out that there was more than one goalpost all along. If someone said, “Once a machine proves a novel mathematical theorem, I’ll agree that it’s generally intelligent,” and then demanded that it run a cafe, that would be moving the goalposts. They ought to acknowledge that their original test has been met.

But general intelligence is a claim about breadth. Proving mathematical results is an extraordinary capability, and it may be evidence for general intelligence, but it doesn’t by itself establish that breadth. Running a cafe involves quite a different collection of abilities: planning, dealing with people, responding to unexpected problems, and keeping things working over time. Something can be very difficult without being a comprehensive test of intelligence.

I wouldn’t want to make running a cafe the definitive test either. The question is whether the system can transfer its abilities across unfamiliar situations, rather than whether it can do this particular thing. And we should keep that separate from whether it’s transformative or dangerous. A system could have enormous consequences through its mathematical or scientific abilities well before it could reliably run a cafe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether running a café is a fair test of general intelligence, but does not state that people expected AI to be able to run one by the time it could prove expert-level novel mathematical results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a reasonable concern there. If someone says that proving a difficult new mathematical result would demonstrate general intelligence, and then, when a system does it, says, “Ah, but can it run a cafe?”, they owe us an explanation of why their criterion has changed. We shouldn’t just keep finding something that humans can do and machines can’t, and putting the finish line there.

But there is a substantive distinction between those tasks. Mathematics can be extraordinarily difficult while still having a relatively clear objective and a way of checking whether you’ve succeeded. Running a cafe involves dealing with a whole collection of less clearly specified problems: suppliers, customers, equipment breaking, people not turning up. You need to notice what needs doing, and adapt when your original plan stops working.

So I’d take novel mathematical research as very strong evidence of an important kind of intelligence. Whether it establishes general intelligence depends on what else the system can do. The cafe example can help make that question concrete, but I wouldn’t make it a necessary test. And certainly we shouldn’t assume that a system has to be able to run a cafe before it can have enormous consequences for the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses running a café as a possible shifted criterion after mathematical results, but does not state that people had expected AI to run one by the time it could prove such results.
